slides.title: Group Actions
slides.notes: Open by placing actions between the Cayley graph chapter and the coming quasi-isometry chapter. A group action is the mechanism that lets algebra move a space, and this lecture follows printed pages 75 through 114 while using original diagrams and diagnostics from the chapter notebook.

slides.title: Action Grammar
slides.notes: Start with the grammar before examples. The homomorphism to an automorphism group is the compact definition, while the pointwise action law is the calculation interface students will actually use. Keep both visible so later stabilizer, quotient, and ping-pong statements do not feel like new notation.

slides.title: Free Actions
slides.notes: Use the two rows of the visual to separate free actions on sets from free actions on graphs. On vertices, a nonidentity element cannot leave a point unmoved. On graphs, the stronger convention also prohibits flipping an edge setwise, which is exactly where order-two generators create trouble.

slides.title: Orbits And Stabilizers
slides.notes: Treat the square as a small laboratory for the orbit-stabilizer relationship. Moving a corner by all symmetries produces four corners, while only two symmetries preserve the selected corner. The center behaves differently because every symmetry fixes it, so stabilizers record hidden redundancy in the motion.

slides.title: Counting With Fixed Sets
slides.notes: Present the counting formula as a change of viewpoint rather than a trick. Counting orbits directly can be messy, but averaging fixed points over group elements lets each symmetry contribute a measurable number. The ledger visual is deliberately synthetic and is meant to train the double-counting reflex.

slides.title: Transitive Graph Actions
slides.notes: This slide explains why transitive graph actions recover Cayley graphs. Choose a base vertex, identify every other vertex with the unique group element carrying the base there, then read adjacent base-neighbors as generators. A path in the graph becomes a word in those generators.

slides.title: Free Groups Act On Trees
slides.notes: State the central equivalence with the tree picture in view. One direction is familiar from free groups and their Cayley trees. The reverse direction is more geometric: a free action on a tree has enough structure to build a Cayley tree and therefore recover a free generating set.

slides.title: Spanning Trees For Actions
slides.notes: Explain the spanning tree as a fundamental set of orbit representatives, not as an arbitrary red subgraph. The action translates this tree through the ambient tree. When each translate is collapsed, the remaining essential edges become the generator candidates in the proof that the acting group is free.

slides.title: Subgroups Of Free Groups
slides.notes: Use Nielsen-Schreier as the payoff for geometric thinking. A subgroup of a free group inherits the free action on the original Cayley tree. The theorem from the previous slide then turns an algebraic subgroup question into the geometry of a restricted tree action.

slides.title: Ping-Pong Domains
slides.notes: Introduce ping-pong as a proof machine for freeness. Each generator has a domain that attracts everything outside the opposite domain. If the domains are disjoint, a reduced word has a visible last move and cannot collapse to the identity because it sends a test point into a prescribed region.

slides.title: Reduced Words Have A Last Domain
slides.notes: Use this slide to rehearse the proof without drowning in notation. Read the word from right to left as a sequence of forced domain transfers. The final letter determines the final domain, so a nonempty reduced word moves the chosen point and therefore represents a nontrivial group element.

slides.title: Matrix Ping-Pong In SL(2,Z)
slides.notes: Connect the abstract domains to a concrete matrix group. The shear matrices act on slopes by fractional linear transformations, and large powers push most slopes toward their favored regions. The point is not numerical magic; it is the same ping-pong mechanism now visible on the projective line.

slides.title: Large-Girth Quotient Graphs
slides.notes: Frame the graph application as a diagnostic consequence of freeness plus finite quotients. A short cycle in a quotient Cayley graph would represent a short relation. Residual finiteness lets one choose a quotient where the relevant short nontrivial words remain nontrivial, forcing the graph to have large girth.

slides.title: Linear Groups And Eigenline Ping-Pong
slides.notes: Use the eigenline diagram to prepare the Tits-alternative outlook. Hyperbolic or proximal matrices have attracting and repelling directions in projective space. When two elements place these directions in separated regions, powers of the elements satisfy ping-pong and generate a free subgroup.

slides.title: Action Diagnostics
slides.notes: Turn the chapter into a checklist students can run on any proposed action. Verify the action law, inspect stabilizers and fixed sets, test freeness on vertices and edges, identify orbit representatives, and then ask whether ping-pong domains or a tree action certify freeness.

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by reconnecting the chapter vocabulary. Actions translate algebra into motion, orbits and stabilizers expose quotient bookkeeping, free tree actions characterize free groups, and ping-pong gives a reusable way to prove free subgroups in matrix settings. The next chapter adds coarse metric control to these actions.
